chief_complaint: fevers, joint pain, positional dyspnea, and diastolic tumor plop
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with fevers, joint pain, positional dyspnea, and diastolic tumor plop. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has developed a severe form of rheumatoid arthritis or an autoimmune disorder that is inflaming both her joints and her lungs.
concerns: She is worried that shifting positions in bed at night will completely block off her breathing and suffocate her in her sleep.
expectations: She hopes to have blood work done to check for inflammation and receive medication so she can sleep lying flat again.

investigation_events.title: Urgent echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent echocardiogram report is now available.

results.value: 4.5 x 3.0 cm pedunculated left-atrial mass attached to the interatrial septum, prolapsing through the mitral valve during diastole

clinical_knowledge.topic: Left Atrial Myxoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Left Atrial Myxoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Left Atrial Myxoma: Urgent echocardiogram, transfer to cardiothoracic surgery for excision, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Left Atrial Myxoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Infective endocarditis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Positional syncope — suggests significant valve obstruction.
management_principles: Plan for Left Atrial Myxoma: Urgent echocardiogram, transfer to cardiothoracic surgery for excision
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A benign primary cardiac tumor causing fevers, joint pain (mimicking systemic illness), and positional breathlessness from a 'tumor plop' sound as it prolapses across the mitral valve.
red_flags: Positional syncope — suggests significant valve obstruction

must_ask.say: Does your breathlessness change with your position?
Have you had fevers or joint pain?
How long has this been going on?
Any sudden weakness or vision changes?

history.answer: I have been having fevers and aching in my joints for the past month, and I've also been getting unusually out of breath.
The fever began about four weeks ago and has been coming and going almost every day.
My temperature usually rises to around 100 degrees Fahrenheit in the late afternoon with mild chills, but never severe shaking.
I took acetaminophen occasionally, and it lowered the fever for a few hours, but it always returned the next day.
My shortness of breath gets noticeably worse when I sit upright or stand up, and it improves whenever I lie flat.
No, I have not had any cough, phlegm, runny nose, or sore throat.
I have no pain or burning when urinating, no need to pee more often, and no side or back pain.
I have not had any stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or loose stools.
No severe headaches, no stiffness in my neck, and no confusion or lightheaded spells.
Both of my knees and wrists have been aching for about three weeks, but they are not red, warm, or swollen.
I haven't noticed any rashes, black scabs, or insect bites on my skin.
I wake up damp with sweat sometimes at night, and I have lost about two pounds over the last month because of a low appetite.
I have not felt any lumps or swollen glands in my neck, armpits, or groin.
I have not traveled outside the area, I don't go hiking or farm, and I don't have pets or handle animals.
No one at home or among my friends has been sick with a fever or any infection.
I have never had chemotherapy, and I do not take steroids or medications that weaken the immune system.
I have never had any heart disease or valve conditions, and I haven't had any dental cleanings or dental surgery recently.
No, I have not started any new prescription pills or over-the-counter supplements lately.
I have been with my husband for decades, and I have never used intravenous or recreational drugs.
I feel mildly lightheaded if I stand up too quickly, but I have never actually passed out or blacked out.
I have not experienced any sudden weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, vision changes, or cold, painful fingers or toes.
I feel thoroughly exhausted and worn out throughout the day, even after a full night of rest.
With the achy joints and the fevers, I assumed I had some sort of aggressive arthritis or autoimmune disease attacking my body.
I'm terrified that when I shift positions in bed at night, my breath will get completely cut off and I won't wake up.
I'm hoping to get some blood tests done for inflammation and medication so I can finally lie down and sleep without suffocating.
I have always been healthy and have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been hospitalized.
I only take a daily multivitamin and an occasional acetaminophen for aches or fever.
I have no known allergies to any medicines, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked, and I only have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I am a retired school administrator and live comfortably at home with my husband.
I went through menopause naturally at age fifty-one and have had no vaginal bleeding or spotting since.
My parents lived into their eighties with no history of heart tumors, heart problems, or autoimmune diseases.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 37.9°C.
Patient appears fatigued and mildly uncomfortable when sitting upright, but is in no acute distress.
Oropharynx is clear without mucosal erythema, tonsillar exudate, or petechiae.
Bilateral tympanic membranes are pearly gray, translucent, and intact with normal landmarks.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or submandibular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no adventitious sounds.
Regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; an early diastolic tumor plop followed by a low-pitched mid-diastolic murmur is heard at the apex, which changes intensity when changing position.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended without guarding or rigidity.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly palpable below the costal margins.
Skin is warm and dry without rashes, eschars, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, or Osler nodes.
Neck is supple with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Bilateral wrists and knees have full range of motion with mild diffuse tenderness, but without erythema, warmth, or swelling.
